subject: Performance SLO & Context Window follow-up — FinCo
messages:
From: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.com>
To: Michael Brewer <michael.brewer@finco.com>, Anna Lopez <anna.lopez@finco.com>
Cc: Rishi Malhotra <rishi.malhotra@redwood.com>, David Kim <david.kim@redwood.com>
Date: Fri, 25 Jun 2027 15:08:00 -0700
Subject: Performance SLO & Context Window follow-up — FinCo

Hi Michael / Anna —

Thanks again for taking the time today. Quick recap from our discovery so we’re aligned and to keep momentum on the PoC kickoff: 

Summary of what I heard from your team: 
- Primary SLO: P99 latency target for inference <= 300ms for the majority of requests (see caveats below).
- Typical request shape: input context ranges from 1k–25k tokens (peak), average around ~4k tokens; expected generation length 256–1024 tokens depending on use case.
- Concurrency & throughput: sustained concurrency target ~50 simultaneous requests during peak, burst to 150 for short periods.
- Streaming: yes — you require partial-token streaming for progressive UX (first-byte / first-chunk latency is important).
- Quality: you need production-grade outputs; no heavy hallucination tolerance.

Key tradeoffs we flagged on the call:
- Larger context windows (16k–32k) increase latency per request and reduce batching efficiency; we can mitigate with KV caching, request sharding, and model variants optimized for long context.
- Strict P99 of 300ms is achievable for smaller context sizes (<=4k) with low-quantization, low-batch paths; for 16k+ contexts we recommend relaxed P99 or a different SLA tier.

Attachments I’m including: finco_latency_requirements.xlsx (your XLS that we annotated) and redwood_poc_plan.pdf (PoC proposal & milestones). I also attached example_payloads.jsonl so your engineering team can see expected request formats.

Proposed next steps: 
1) You share 1–2 sample payloads and a short traffic profile (qps by hour, average request size, percent of streaming sessions).
2) We run a short benchmark (Redwood-hosted) against two model variants: rlm-16k-low-latency and rlm-32k-quant to show latency/throughput tradeoffs for your payloads.
3) PoC kickoff: week of 2027-07-05 (proposed 2027-07-06). We’ll scope a 2-week PoC focusing on the 50-concurrency baseline and streaming experience.

Can you confirm the P99 target (300ms) applies to end-to-end first-byte streaming latency vs full-response completion? Also confirm whether the 1024 token upper-bound is a hard limit for outputs.

I cc’d Rishi and David from our infra/perf team who will be involved in benchmarking and PoC design.

Thanks —
Marissa
Senior Sales Engineer | Redwood Inference
marissa.cole@redwood.com | +1 (415) 555-0123

Date: Sat, 26 Jun 2027 09:22:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Performance SLO & Context Window follow-up — FinCo

Thanks Marissa — this is great context. A couple clarifying Qs before we kick off the PoC: 

1) When you say P99 <= 300ms, are you referring to first-byte streaming latency (i.e., time to first chunk) or time to final token (end-to-end)? Our UX team is primarily worried about time-to-first-chunk but legal wants a clear SLA definition.
2) For output length: the 1024 token figure is a reasonable upper bound for the worst-case, but 256 tokens is more common. We can commit to the distribution in the sample payloads.
3) For long-context requests (~20–25k tokens), is there an operational pattern you recommend (summarization on-client, chunking + retrieval, or a larger-model variant)?

We’re comfortable with the proposed PoC dates. If you can confirm the above and share the benchmark plan I’ll get our infra engineer (Anna) to pull sample payloads and traffic.

Subject: Re: Performance SLO & Context Window follow-up — FinCo

Hi Michael —

Great questions; quick answers and some concrete guidance: 

1) SLA interpretation: We recommend defining two SLOs for clarity:
   - First-byte streaming SLO (P99) = 300ms — covers UX responsiveness (time to first chunk).
   - Completion SLO (tail P99) = 600ms for full response when outputs are <=512 tokens; for outputs >512 tokens expect higher completion latency and we’ll show numbers in the benchmark.

2) Output distribution: thanks — assume 256 tokens typical and 1024 tokens worst-case for benchmarking.

3) Long-context (20k+): recommended approaches:
   - Retrieval-augmented chunking + relevance filtering (client-side or pre-processing) to reduce immediate context size.
   - KV cache + model with native 32k context for sessions that truly need full history (we’ll show latency/throughput tradeoffs).

Model variants & tradeoffs we’ll test in the benchmark: 
- rlm-16k-low-latency: optimized kernel path for <=16k inputs, lower quantization, better P99 at the expense of higher cost.
- rlm-32k-quant: supports 32k contexts with quantized weights for cost efficiency; expect higher P99 and variance in tail latency.

What we need from you to run an accurate benchmark:
- 50–150 concurrent session profile (CSV or simple histogram),
- 100 sample payloads reflecting token-size distribution,
- Any constraints on throughput (per-minute or per-hour limits) and expected percent of streaming sessions.

I’ll put together a short benchmarking plan and timeline and share it by EOD Monday. If you’re ok, we’ll schedule a 30-min technical sync for 2027-07-06 to kickoff the PoC.

Thanks —
Marissa

Looping you in — forwarding FinCo notes. Quick internal notes for engineering: 
- Prioritize first-byte streaming path optimizations (fast first-token generation) since they asked for a 300ms P99.
- For 16k+ contexts, plan to test KV cache hit rates and a hybrid split strategy (serve hot state with 16k fast model, fall back to 32k as needed).
- Batching: at 50 concurrent sessions we can benefit from micro-batching; for bursts to 150 we should ensure autoscale and prewarming behavior in the PoC.

Marissa — I’ll start drafting the benchmark harness (sample size, qps profile, token distribution) and share by Monday.

Rishi
Principal Infra Engineer | Redwood Inference
